Livestock lockdown

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Foot-and-mouth disease didn’t defeat South Africa’s livestock industry, delay did, in a system where permission mattered more than prevention

Unique Selling Point:
This investigation exposes how South Africa’s worst animal-health disaster is unfolding as the cure is trapped by bureaucracy and the greed embedded in a system that controls it.


Summary:
Foot-and-mouth disease in South Africa has crossed a critical threshold. What began as a series of outbreaks has evolved into an endemic crisis affecting multiple provinces, collapsing livestock markets, and threatening food security. Experts warn the country may not yet have reached the peak of the outbreak. South Africa currently has SAT-1, SAT-2 and SAT-3 strains circulating, with sheep and pigs now also affected, widening the crisis beyond cattle.
South Africa has an estimated 14 million cattle, of which approximately 5 million are communal cattle. For millions of households, especially in rural areas, livestock functions as a bank. Cattle are sold to buy food, pay school fees, and cover medical bills. Quarantine restrictions, which can last up to a year, prevent farmers from selling animals while costs continue to rise. Livestock must still be fed and maintained, but without income. Auctions have been postponed for months, leaving farmers with no route to market. Many describe the situation as a COVID-style lockdown for cattle farmers, except this time there is no relief fund, no safety net, and no timeline.
South Africa requires an estimated 100 million vaccine doses immediately, followed by another 100 million within three months, to suppress transmission. Yet the state-owned manufacturer, Onderstepoort Biological Products (OBP), is unable to meet this demand. Between 1984 and 2006, OBP successfully produced foot-and-mouth vaccines, but these were based on virus strains circulating at the time. Since then, the virus has mutated. New strains emerged, but updated genetic material was not submitted timeously to the international reference laboratory in the United Kingdom, where strain confirmation and vaccine matching are conducted. As a member of the World Organisation for Animal Health, South Africa is expected to submit this material, but industry stakeholders allege this was delayed to retain intellectual property control. The department disputes aspects of this timeline, stating samples are being prepared, but infections continue to spread.

An Argentinian manufacturer with decades of experience in foot-and-mouth disease control has licensed a South African private company to distribute vaccines compatible with earlier strains. These vaccines could be imported under Section 21 of South Africa’s medicines legislation. However, even if regulatory approval is granted, import permits require authorisation by the Director of Animal Health. That authority currently rests with a single office, and industry stakeholders allege that approvals have stalled during the most critical phase of the crisis. In the absence of decisive leadership, pressure has mounted to route all vaccine supply through OBP, despite its inability to produce at scale.
The human cost is escalating. Large commercial dairy farms have become sites of mass animal burials. A volunteer-run crisis hotline has been established to deal with suicide threats from farmers facing financial ruin. Critics argue the state has normalised the outbreak rather than stopped it, leaving farmers powerless, animals suffering, and livelihoods destroyed.



Further information:
Under South African law, farmers are prohibited from independently vaccinating against foot-and-mouth disease. All vaccination, imports, and emergency approvals are controlled by the Department of Agriculture, with final authority vested in the Director of Animal Health. Industry stakeholders allege that during the most critical phase of the outbreak, emergency approvals stalled, task-team recommendations were rejected, and no alternative delegation mechanism was activated.
In 2011, R500 million was allocated to Onderstepoort Biological Products for infrastructure and development, yet there is no clear public accounting of how that funding was spent. Despite more than a decade of research into local strains, OBP’s infrastructure has deteriorated to the point where it cannot meet national vaccine demand. Meanwhile, the department has refused to license private manufacturers to produce vaccines locally and has not issued permits for large-scale vaccine imports, citing biosecurity concerns. Critics argue this has effectively preserved a state monopoly while the outbreak worsened.
Last year, the Minister of Agriculture appointed a task team of scientists and veterinarians with a combined 200 years of experience to advise on solutions. According to multiple sources, key recommendations were not adopted, and senior officials did not attend meetings. The minister publicly stated that the entire country would be vaccinated, a declaration task-team members say was made without consultation and without a clear operational plan. As the crisis deepened, the minister attended overseas engagements, including agricultural conferences, while South Africa faced its worst animal-health outbreak on record.
Foot-and-mouth disease is one of the most contagious livestock diseases in the world, with devastating consequences for trade, food supply, and rural economies. South Africa historically relied on strict movement controls, rapid vaccination, and centralised oversight to contain outbreaks. Repeated failures to enforce movement restrictions allowed the virus to spread between provinces. Once that containment line collapsed, vaccination became the only viable tool left. Instead, the system remains locked in process.
This investigation follows the paper trail, the legal framework, and the human cost of a response where speed mattered, but permission never came.

Summary: Foot-and-mouth disease in South Africa has crossed a critical threshold. What began as a series of outbreaks has evolved into an endemic crisis affecting multiple provinces, collapsing livestock markets, and threatening food security. Experts warn the country may not yet have reached the peak of the outbreak. South Africa currently has SAT-1, SAT-2 and SAT-3 strains circulating, with sheep and pigs now also affected, widening the crisis beyond cattle. South Africa has an estimated 14 million cattle, of which approximately 5 million are communal cattle. For millions of households, especially in rural areas, livestock functions as a bank. Cattle are sold to buy food, pay school fees, and cover medical bills. Quarantine restrictions, which can last up to a year, prevent farmers from selling animals while costs continue to rise. Livestock must still be fed and maintained, but without income. Auctions have been postponed for months, leaving farmers with no route to market. Many describe the situation as a COVID-style lockdown for cattle farmers, except this time there is no relief fund, no safety net, and no timeline. South Africa requires an estimated 100 million vaccine doses immediately, followed by another 100 million within three months, to suppress transmission. Yet the state-owned manufacturer, Onderstepoort Biological Products (OBP), is unable to meet this demand. Between 1984 and 2006, OBP successfully produced foot-and-mouth vaccines, but these were based on virus strains circulating at the time. Since then, the virus has mutated. New strains emerged, but updated genetic material was not submitted timeously to the international reference laboratory in the United Kingdom, where strain confirmation and vaccine matching are conducted. As a member of the World Organisation for Animal Health, South Africa is expected to submit this material, but industry stakeholders allege this was delayed to retain intellectual property control. The department disputes aspects of this timeline, stating samples are being prepared, but infections continue to spread. An Argentinian manufacturer with decades of experience in foot-and-mouth disease control has licensed a South African private company to distribute vaccines compatible with earlier strains. These vaccines could be imported under Section 21 of South Africa’s medicines legislation. However, even if regulatory approval is granted, import permits require authorisation by the Director of Animal Health. That authority currently rests with a single office, and industry stakeholders allege that approvals have stalled during the most critical phase of the crisis. In the absence of decisive leadership, pressure has mounted to route all vaccine supply through OBP, despite its inability to produce at scale. The human cost is escalating. Large commercial dairy farms have become sites of mass animal burials. A volunteer-run crisis hotline has been established to deal with suicide threats from farmers facing financial ruin. Critics argue the state has normalised the outbreak rather than stopped it, leaving farmers powerless, animals suffering, and livelihoods destroyed. Further information: Under South African law, farmers are prohibited from independently vaccinating against foot-and-mouth disease. All vaccination, imports, and emergency approvals are controlled by the Department of Agriculture, with final authority vested in the Director of Animal Health. Industry stakeholders allege that during the most critical phase of the outbreak, emergency approvals stalled, task-team recommendations were rejected, and no alternative delegation mechanism was activated. In 2011, R500 million was allocated to Onderstepoort Biological Products for infrastructure and development, yet there is no clear public accounting of how that funding was spent. Despite more than a decade of research into local strains, OBP’s infrastructure has deteriorated to the point where it cannot meet national vaccine demand. Meanwhile, the department has refused to license private manufacturers to produce vaccines locally and has not issued permits for large-scale vaccine imports, citing biosecurity concerns. Critics argue this has effectively preserved a state monopoly while the outbreak worsened. Last year, the Minister of Agriculture appointed a task team of scientists and veterinarians with a combined 200 years of experience to advise on solutions. According to multiple sources, key recommendations were not adopted, and senior officials did not attend meetings. The minister publicly stated that the entire country would be vaccinated, a declaration task-team members say was made without consultation and without a clear operational plan. As the crisis deepened, the minister attended overseas engagements, including agricultural conferences, while South Africa faced its worst animal-health outbreak on record. Foot-and-mouth disease is one of the most contagious livestock diseases in the world, with devastating consequences for trade, food supply, and rural economies. South Africa historically relied on strict movement controls, rapid vaccination, and centralised oversight to contain outbreaks. Repeated failures to enforce movement restrictions allowed the virus to spread between provinces. Once that containment line collapsed, vaccination became the only viable tool left. Instead, the system remains locked in process. This investigation follows the paper trail, the legal framework, and the human cost of a response where speed mattered, but permission never came. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Foot-and-mouth disease didn’t defeat South Africa’s livestock industry, delay did, in a system where permission mattered more than prevention
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This investigation exposes how South Africa’s worst animal-health disaster is unfolding as the cure is trapped by bureaucracy and the greed embedded in a system that controls it.
metadata.Summary: Foot-and-mouth disease in South Africa has crossed a critical threshold. What began as a series of outbreaks has evolved into an endemic crisis affecting multiple provinces, collapsing livestock markets, and threatening food security. Experts warn the country may not yet have reached the peak of the outbreak. South Africa currently has SAT-1, SAT-2 and SAT-3 strains circulating, with sheep and pigs now also affected, widening the crisis beyond cattle. South Africa has an estimated 14 million cattle, of which approximately 5 million are communal cattle. For millions of households, especially in rural areas, livestock functions as a bank. Cattle are sold to buy food, pay school fees, and cover medical bills. Quarantine restrictions, which can last up to a year, prevent farmers from selling animals while costs continue to rise. Livestock must still be fed and maintained, but without income. Auctions have been postponed for months, leaving farmers with no route to market. Many describe the situation as a COVID-style lockdown for cattle farmers, except this time there is no relief fund, no safety net, and no timeline. South Africa requires an estimated 100 million vaccine doses immediately, followed by another 100 million within three months, to suppress transmission. Yet the state-owned manufacturer, Onderstepoort Biological Products (OBP), is unable to meet this demand. Between 1984 and 2006, OBP successfully produced foot-and-mouth vaccines, but these were based on virus strains circulating at the time. Since then, the virus has mutated. New strains emerged, but updated genetic material was not submitted timeously to the international reference laboratory in the United Kingdom, where strain confirmation and vaccine matching are conducted. As a member of the World Organisation for Animal Health, South Africa is expected to submit this material, but industry stakeholders allege this was delayed to retain intellectual property control. The department disputes aspects of this timeline, stating samples are being prepared, but infections continue to spread. An Argentinian manufacturer with decades of experience in foot-and-mouth disease control has licensed a South African private company to distribute vaccines compatible with earlier strains. These vaccines could be imported under Section 21 of South Africa’s medicines legislation. However, even if regulatory approval is granted, import permits require authorisation by the Director of Animal Health. That authority currently rests with a single office, and industry stakeholders allege that approvals have stalled during the most critical phase of the crisis. In the absence of decisive leadership, pressure has mounted to route all vaccine supply through OBP, despite its inability to produce at scale. The human cost is escalating. Large commercial dairy farms have become sites of mass animal burials. A volunteer-run crisis hotline has been established to deal with suicide threats from farmers facing financial ruin. Critics argue the state has normalised the outbreak rather than stopped it, leaving farmers powerless, animals suffering, and livelihoods destroyed.
metadata.Further information: Under South African law, farmers are prohibited from independently vaccinating against foot-and-mouth disease. All vaccination, imports, and emergency approvals are controlled by the Department of Agriculture, with final authority vested in the Director of Animal Health. Industry stakeholders allege that during the most critical phase of the outbreak, emergency approvals stalled, task-team recommendations were rejected, and no alternative delegation mechanism was activated. In 2011, R500 million was allocated to Onderstepoort Biological Products for infrastructure and development, yet there is no clear public accounting of how that funding was spent. Despite more than a decade of research into local strains, OBP’s infrastructure has deteriorated to the point where it cannot meet national vaccine demand. Meanwhile, the department has refused to license private manufacturers to produce vaccines locally and has not issued permits for large-scale vaccine imports, citing biosecurity concerns. Critics argue this has effectively preserved a state monopoly while the outbreak worsened. Last year, the Minister of Agriculture appointed a task team of scientists and veterinarians with a combined 200 years of experience to advise on solutions. According to multiple sources, key recommendations were not adopted, and senior officials did not attend meetings. The minister publicly stated that the entire country would be vaccinated, a declaration task-team members say was made without consultation and without a clear operational plan. As the crisis deepened, the minister attended overseas engagements, including agricultural conferences, while South Africa faced its worst animal-health outbreak on record. Foot-and-mouth disease is one of the most contagious livestock diseases in the world, with devastating consequences for trade, food supply, and rural economies. South Africa historically relied on strict movement controls, rapid vaccination, and centralised oversight to contain outbreaks. Repeated failures to enforce movement restrictions allowed the virus to spread between provinces. Once that containment line collapsed, vaccination became the only viable tool left. Instead, the system remains locked in process. This investigation follows the paper trail, the legal framework, and the human cost of a response where speed mattered, but permission never came.
